---
title: "Security, Privacy, and AI Artifact Custody"
unit_id: "unit-04"
---

A paper arrives with more than an argument. Its supporting package includes a
small evaluation script, a model adapter, a configuration file, example
prompts, and a link to downloadable weights. The request sounds routine: add
the paper to the book, run the example, preserve the useful result, and publish
the update.

Every noun in that sentence hides a different boundary. The paper may be safe
to read while its examples contain hostile instructions. The script may be
correctly signed while importing a compromised dependency. The adapter may be
harmless in isolation while changing the behavior of a model that can use
tools. The prompts may include personal or confidential data that the author
had authority to study but not to redistribute. The weights may be available
to download without being authorized for this machine, this purpose, or a
public derivative. A successful local run may establish none of those facts.

The easy mistake is to ask one broad question: is the package secure? No single
mechanism can answer it. A sandbox can limit some effects but cannot decide
whether the data use is legitimate. Encryption can protect bytes while an
authorized program misuses them. A signature can identify an issuer without
proving that the artifact is benign. An attestation can describe a measured
environment without establishing that the right policy ran for the right
person. A model card can document release intentions without recalling a copy
once usable weights are public.

The stack needs a set of narrower questions that meet at explicit transitions.
Who is asking? What exact object is involved? What operation is permitted? What
data may enter? Which effects may leave? What evidence is current? Which copy,
key, dependency, or recipient is still under control? What happens when the
answer is unknown? The purpose of the security layer is not to produce a
single reassuring verdict. It is to prevent one favorable fact from silently
authorizing everything around it.

The previous chapter established the separation between proposing an effect
and possessing authority to cause it. This chapter moves beneath that boundary.
It asks what the runtime, data, artifacts, and release process must preserve so
that the authority distinction remains real when the model, its inputs, or its
dependencies are untrusted.

## A Change Can Be Correct and Still Be Unsafe

Suppose the paper's script produces exactly the output described by its author.
That is useful evidence about reproducibility under the observed configuration.
It does not answer whether the script read files outside its task, sent data
over the network, persisted credentials, loaded a different model derivative,
or wrote output to a public location. Correct computation and authorized
computation are different properties.

The distinction matters more for AI systems because natural-language content
can influence control flow. A source document can contain an instruction that
the model mistakes for part of its task. A retrieved web page can ask the model
to reveal its context. A tool description can induce a call whose arguments
carry confidential material. A planner can discover a route that satisfies the
surface request while violating the operator's unstated assumptions. The model
does not need malicious intent for any of this to happen. Ambiguous channels
and excessive authority are enough.

Security therefore starts from a threat model and an authority-use
transaction, not from trust in the prompt. The transaction identifies the
principal, purpose, operation, target, data scope, destination, budget, time,
policy, and revocation authority. It admits only the context and capabilities
needed for that operation. It mediates effects as they occur. It treats any
output that might carry protected information as tainted until a separate
declassification decision permits release. It closes temporary files, handles,
caches, logs, descendants, and unresolved residuals when the work ends.

In the paper-ingestion case, reading the manuscript and running its script are
separate grants. The reader may receive a sanitized source note while the
execution environment receives a temporary checkout, a synthetic fixture, and
no access to private source archives. The model may propose a repository patch,
but a reference monitor decides which files it can read and write. The test may
produce a result, but a declassifier decides whether logs and artifacts can
leave the compartment. The final publication action remains outside the
experiment entirely.

That separation may seem fussy until one remembers what a failure looks like.
A secret copied into a log can survive after the process exits. An opaque
credential handle can be replayed even when its bytes were never shown. A
temporary model load can leave plaintext pages in host memory, swap, a crash
dump, or an accelerator allocation. A denial that arrives after an external
write has already happened is not enforcement. The system has to control the
transition before the irreversible part, not explain it afterward.

## The Smallest Powerful Kernel

The security kernel should be narrow because anything inside it can invalidate
the larger system. Its job is not to reason about every domain. It is to make a
small set of facts non-optional: exact identity, live authority, policy version,
time and freshness, context provenance, artifact custody, observed effects,
evaluation scope, isolation boundary, rollback coverage, and release identity.
Each fact needs a failure consequence.

If the target artifact is ambiguous, the load is held. If the policy is stale,
the grant is not reused. If the runtime cannot observe a material effect, the
claim narrows or execution stops. If rollback cannot cover an external action,
the residual remains open. If a proposed release does not match the artifact
that was reviewed, publication is blocked. The point is not to fill fields. It
is to ensure that missing facts change what the system can do.

A Digital SCIF is one expression of this idea: a temporary compartment with a
declared isolation grade, minimized context, mediated tools, controlled egress,
and explicit closure. The name is deliberately evocative, but the name itself
guarantees nothing. A process sandbox may share a kernel, network, browser
profile, accelerator, operator, or cloud control plane. A virtual machine may
still expose side channels or depend on a compromised host. The compartment's
claim is only as wide as the surfaces actually isolated and observed.

The useful pattern is late substitution. If a task needs a credential, the
ordinary model context receives a constrained handle rather than raw secret
bytes. A privileged component checks the live lease and substitutes the secret
at the narrow point of use. This reduces exposure, but it does not make the
handle harmless. Handles can be stolen, redirected, correlated, or replayed.
They need purpose, destination, use-count, expiry, and revocation constraints
of their own.

Declassification is equally important. A model can transform protected data
without reproducing it verbatim. It may reveal an inference, a membership
signal, a sensitive aggregate, or an actionable description. An output filter
that searches only for literal strings is therefore not a general privacy
boundary. The declassification decision must know what entered, what operation
was permitted, what the output means for the recipient, and which uncertainty
remains.

The kernel should also preserve bounded liveness. A system that blocks every
uncertain action can be secure in a narrow sense while becoming unusable and
encouraging bypass. Denials need named reasons, appeal or repair routes, and
measured false-refusal cost. Stable low-risk operations should compile into
cheap policies. Novel, high-consequence, or poorly observed operations should
receive more scrutiny. Security has to compete on the joint frontier of useful
work, disclosure, unauthorized effects, availability, recovery, human burden,
and cost.

## The Model Is Part of the Attack Surface

Even a perfect reference monitor needs a threat description for the learned
component it is mediating. Models can fail differently across training,
adaptation, inference, retrieval, multimodal inputs, tool use, and model access.
An adversary may know the architecture, query only an API, control a fraction
of training data, supply a trigger, perturb one sensor, or adapt after seeing a
defense. Calling all of these “adversarial AI” hides the mechanism that a
control is supposed to address.

A model-threat contract therefore binds the exact checkpoint and serving
configuration to the lifecycle stage, attacker's knowledge and capability,
access, objective, budget, adaptation, success criterion, observed effect,
detector, mitigation, utility cost, recovery, disclosure, and residual. A
failed attack has meaning only inside that envelope. It may show that one
implementation did not achieve one objective with one budget. It does not show
that the model is robust.

The same discipline prevents defense laundering. A regional certificate can
establish a property over a bounded network and input region without covering
poisoning, model extraction, a tool chain, or a different checkpoint. A runtime
monitor can detect a class of behavior without proving that it sees every
relevant path. Recovery can repair a damaged artifact without preventing the
attack. These mechanisms can reinforce one another, but they are not
substitutes.

For the incoming paper, the first question is whether its examples are data or
instructions. The second is whether its script or adapter changes the model's
attack surface. The third is whether the evaluation includes an attacker that
knows about the proposed defense. The fourth is whether a failed exploit left
utility, recovery, or disclosure costs unmeasured. The output of that review is
a bounded threat disposition consumed by the kernel. It does not replace the
kernel's authority decision.

This division of labor matters. Adversarial evaluation tells the system what
learned behavior was challenged and what remained unresolved. The kernel
decides whether a particular model may receive a particular capability inside
a particular route. A robust model can still be over-authorized. A fragile
model can sometimes perform a harmless, tightly mediated task. Neither result
should be promoted into the other.

## Privacy Is About Use, Not Merely Secrecy

Security asks whether an operation stayed inside its permitted technical
boundary. Privacy asks a broader and more human question: was this information
use legitimate, minimized, bounded to its purpose, and accountable to the
people affected by it? Data can remain encrypted throughout computation and
still be used for an unauthorized purpose. Data can be public and still be
combined, inferred, or retained in ways that create a privacy harm.

An information-lifecycle transaction names the affected person or group, data
categories and sources, purpose, processing operation, claimed authority and
jurisdiction, recipients, retention, minimization decision, cross-user
boundaries, threat model, rights state, remedy, exceptions, known copies,
derivatives, learned influence, cost, and residuals. Not every use needs the
same formal mechanism, but every consequential use needs enough identity to be
challenged and changed.

Consider a deletion request. Removing the source row is not the same as
removing a curated shard, backup, feature table, checkpoint influence, cached
output, or recipient copy. Revoking future ordinary use is not proof that every
byte disappeared. A changed response from the model is not proof of forgetting.
The honest transaction records a separate disposition for each known copy and
keeps unknown copies or influence as residuals.

In the paper-ingestion case, the source note may quote or summarize material
that was legitimately published, while the example data has a different
rights boundary. The system should not infer permission to store prompts from
permission to read the paper. It should not infer permission to train from
permission to evaluate. It should not infer permission to publish logs from
permission to run a local test. Purpose is attached to the transition, not
carried forever by the file.

This is where privacy and the security kernel meet. Privacy decides the
permitted use and required remedy. The kernel enforces the resulting technical
scope. If the privacy record requires that prompts never leave a local trust
domain, the kernel can deny a cloud route. If the kernel cannot observe a
relevant recipient or derivative, privacy cannot pretend the flow is complete.
One owner supplies legitimacy; the other supplies mediation. Neither certifies
the other.

## Protected Computation Is Evidence, Not Permission

Sometimes the declared distrust boundary cannot be removed by ordinary
organizational controls. A data holder may not trust the model provider with
raw records. A model provider may not trust the data holder with proprietary
weights. Both may need evidence that a committed operation ran in a particular
environment. Confidential execution, secure multiparty computation, fully
homomorphic encryption, zero-knowledge proofs, differential privacy, and local
execution address different pieces of this problem.

The right starting point is a guarantee vector. It distinguishes input
confidentiality, model confidentiality, computation integrity, platform
identity, output authenticity, usage privacy, availability, and recovery. It
also names the adversary, trust assumptions, allowed leakage, unsupported
properties, and fallback. Choosing a technology before naming those properties
often protects the wrong asset.

Remote attestation illustrates the boundary. An attester produces evidence
about a measured environment. A verifier appraises that evidence against
reference values and policy. A relying party decides what, if anything, the
result authorizes. Collapsing those roles lets a platform's statement become
its own permission. Keeping them separate makes freshness, verifier
dependencies, reference-value changes, and revocation visible.

Cryptographic proof has a similar semantic limit. A proof may strongly
establish that an encoded relation held for committed values. The system still
has to ask whether the relation represented the intended model, tokenizer,
preprocessing, sampling rule, tool call, or policy. A valid proof of the wrong
relation is valid evidence about the wrong thing. The circuit-to-semantics gap
belongs in the receipt, not in a footnote.

Cost and fallback are also part of the security claim. A protected path that
silently falls back to ordinary inference under load has a different guarantee
from the path that was reviewed. Long queues, memory pressure, proof size,
failure timing, access patterns, and logs can create leakage or denial-of-
service channels. The result should identify which path ran and which
properties survived.

For the paper package, a protected execution receipt could bind the exact
script, model, adapter, configuration, input commitment, environment,
freshness challenge, verifier policy, output commitment, measured cost,
fallback state, and unsupported properties. That would make the run
reconstructible. It would not establish that the paper's data use was lawful,
that the model output was true, or that the result was safe to publish.

## Model Weights Are a Custody Graph

Model weights are not just another dependency file. A capable model can be a
high-value asset, an attack target, a source of proprietary information, and a
capability that becomes difficult to recall once copied. Custody therefore
tracks more than the canonical checkpoint. It follows adapters, quantizations,
distillations, shards, caches, backups, recovery images, optimizer state,
extracted equivalents, recipient copies, and any combination that can
reconstruct a governed capability.

Each custody transition binds exact content and lineage identity, holder,
purpose, location, storage and transfer state, key lifecycle, measured
environment, verifier policy, freshness, requested effect, observed effect,
plaintext exposure, descendants, incident state, sanitization method, recovery,
and residual owner. Decryption, loading, serving, transferring, and publishing
are separate authorities. A key released for one model and environment does not
authorize a repackaged derivative merely because both signatures are valid.

Paging and quantization make the graph more important, not less. A model loaded
from SSD may create encrypted archives, decrypted pages, memory-mapped files,
host buffers, accelerator allocations, swap entries, temporary conversions,
and crash artifacts. A quantized representation may include scales, codebooks,
kernels, calibration data, residuals, and a full-precision fallback. “The
weights are encrypted on disk” says little about these descendants.

Deletion language must remain precise. Cache eviction removes an entry from a
cache policy. File deletion removes a namespace reference. Key revocation can
deny future compliant requests. Cryptographic erase applies under a declared
key and attacker model. Media sanitization applies a method to a declared
medium. Recipient recall asks another party to return or delete material. None
of these operations proves that every copy or reconstruction path is gone.

The running case should therefore keep the downloadable weights quarantined
until their digest, lineage, license, derivative relation, holder, intended
purpose, and load route are explicit. A local experiment can use a harmless
substitute or remain unexecuted. Availability on the internet is not local
authority. A successful test is not permission to retain, redistribute, or
publish a derivative.

## The Supply Chain Is a Living Dependency Graph

Custody asks who controls an artifact. Supply-chain integrity asks what that
artifact depends on, which assertions describe it, and which consumers become
affected when something changes. The graph includes data, code, models,
prompts, policies, build and training steps, environments, hardware and
firmware, suppliers, services, signers, advisories, transformations, releases,
recipients, descendants, retention, and retirement.

A digest can establish that two byte sequences match. A signature can establish
that a key signed a statement. A bill of materials can list components known to
its producer. None proves that the statement is true, the list is complete, the
artifact is correct, the data rights are adequate, or the model is safe. The
graph is valuable because it carries typed claims and invalidations to the
consumers that depend on them, not because metadata itself creates trust.

Suppose the paper's script imports a library that later receives a critical
advisory. The affected path should reach the exact evaluation result, generated
artifact, chapter statement, and release candidate that consumed it. Those
consumers move to a named state such as quarantine or re-review. They do not
remain ordinary because a dashboard has not refreshed. If a patched component
arrives, restoration still requires identity, compatibility, rerun, and
consumer-specific acceptance.

The graph must remain consumer-relative. A training pipeline and a
documentation renderer may depend on the same package but require different
properties. A missing license field may block redistribution without blocking
a local security analysis. A compromised build step may invalidate an
executable artifact while leaving the text of a cited paper intact. Relation
types determine propagation; undifferentiated “tainted” labels create either
false confidence or permanent quarantine.

Completeness is also bounded. Unknown dependencies and unofficial derivatives
remain possible. The system should preserve discovery methods, coverage, and
unknown edges rather than claiming world-complete lineage. A graph that admits
its boundary can guide repair. A graph that calls itself complete by definition
cannot notice what it missed.

## Release Changes the Kind of Control

Before release, custody can often deny a key, stop a transfer, narrow a lease,
or destroy a controlled copy. After usable weights reach independent
recipients, those verbs usually apply only to official hosting, future keys,
licenses, cooperative registries, or parties within legal and technical reach.
Open-weight release is therefore not a weaker setting on the same deployment
control. It is an authority-loss transition.

A serious release case freezes the exact artifact, code, configuration, and
license. It compares release with realistic alternatives such as no release,
hosted access, gated research access, delayed release, or a less capable model.
It tests default behavior, safeguard removal, fine-tuning, merging,
quantization, repackaging, and scaffolded elicitation. It considers marginal
risk relative to what is already accessible, cumulative ecosystem effects,
benefits, access distribution, monitoring, incident channels, patch adoption,
and the controls that survive copying.

This does not create a presumption against open development. Open weights can
support research, access, competition, audit, customization, education, and
local control. Those benefits should be evaluated with the same seriousness as
risks, including who receives them and who bears the residual. The discipline
is symmetric: neither “openness is always good” nor “custody is always safer”
is allowed to replace an artifact- and date-specific comparison.

After release, governance still has work to do. Maintainers can publish
advisories, improve safer derivatives, coordinate registries, support incident
response, update evaluations, and provide patches. Institutions can use law,
norms, procurement, and platform policy within their reach. Researchers can
measure downstream adaptations. What the system cannot honestly claim is
universal recall of independently held usable bytes.

For the incoming package, a link to weights can be recorded without mirroring
or endorsing them. A local reproduction can remain separate from a public
release decision. If the project eventually distributes a derived artifact,
the decision must bind the exact bytes and the evidence current at that time.
The fact that a neighboring project already published something similar is a
comparator, not delegated authority.

## One End-to-End Custody Decision

Return to the original request. The system first ingests the paper as a source,
preserving its public identity and separating reported results from local
evidence. The manuscript enters an untrusted reading context. Any embedded
instructions are treated as data. The model can propose concepts and chapter
routes, but it receives no automatic authority to run code or fetch weights.

The script enters a supply-chain intake. Its digest, license, repository
revision, declared dependencies, build instructions, and expected outputs are
recorded. Dependencies are resolved under a network policy that does not expose
private credentials. Unknown or mutable dependencies hold execution or force a
harmless pinned substitute. A signature, if present, is preserved as one
issuer statement rather than converted into a safety verdict.

The example data enters a privacy review. The system identifies whether it is
synthetic, public, licensed, personal, confidential, or unknown; which purpose
the paper permits; whether local reproduction needs the full granularity; what
may be retained; and what may appear in logs or the final book. If authority is
unclear, the experiment narrows to synthetic data or remains unexecuted. The
book can still discuss the method without fabricating a result.

The model and adapter enter custody review. The exact model family,
checkpoint, tokenizer, adapter, quantization, and serving configuration are
distinguished. The system decides whether downloading is permitted, which
machine and storage tier may hold the artifact, whether decryption or loading
is authorized, how temporary descendants are tracked, and which sanitization
or retention action closes the run. A public link does not waive these steps.

Execution receives a short-lived lease. The compartment contains only the
pinned code, approved data or synthetic fixture, named model artifact or
substitute, bounded compute, required tools, and a destination for temporary
results. Network egress, repository writes, and secret use are denied unless
separately granted. The model can request actions; the monitor mediates them.
Logs and outputs retain taint until the declassifier checks them against the
purpose and publication boundary.

The result then splits into several records. A reproducibility record says what
ran and what was observed. A threat record says which attacks or negative
controls were attempted. A privacy record says what data and derivatives
remain. A custody record says where model artifacts and plaintext descendants
went. A supply-chain record preserves dependencies and invalidation paths. A
publication decision says which text, code, or artifact may leave. None of
these records automatically upgrades the others.

Finally, the repository patch is reviewed as a separate effect. The system can
add a source note and bounded prose while leaving the experiment labeled
unreproduced. It can record a failed run without publishing sensitive logs. It
can preserve an external weight link without hosting the artifact. It can
accept a local result while denying a public derivative. This is not
indecision. It is the ability to produce the largest honest product supported
by the available authority and evidence.

## Failure Cases

The first failure is **security-label laundering**. “Sandboxed,” “encrypted,”
“attested,” “verified,” or “signed” becomes a universal adjective. Each term
has a scope. The remedy is to state the exact property, actor, object,
assumption, freshness condition, and consumer decision it can support.

The second is **metadata without enforcement**. The repository contains rich
leases, threat models, and receipts, but the model can still write through an
unmediated tool or retrieve a secret from ordinary context. A record that does
not change an effect is documentation, not a security boundary.

The third is **incomplete observation**. The process reports a clean run while
network, filesystem, accelerator, browser, or operator channels remain outside
the observer. The honest response is to narrow the isolation claim and retain
the channel as a residual, not to infer safety from silence.

The fourth is **proof-purpose substitution**. A cryptographic proof or
attestation validates its statement, and the system silently treats that as
authorization, privacy, semantic correctness, or output truth. The relying
party must make a separate decision using the exact statement and its policy.

The fifth is **copy-lineage fiction**. One canonical weight file is protected
while quantizations, adapters, backups, memory pages, or recipient copies are
ignored. Revocation then applies to the official route but is described as
recall. Custody needs a derivative closure and an explicit unknown-copy
residual.

The sixth is **provenance theater**. Every component has a digest and signature,
yet harmful or compromised artifacts move through the graph because authentic
assertions were mistaken for true, complete, or adequate ones. Provenance must
connect to independent verification, observed effects, and consumer-specific
policy.

The seventh is **silent fallback**. Protected computation fails under realistic
load and the service quietly routes to an unprotected path. The user receives
an answer with a different guarantee from the one requested. Fallback must be
observable, separately authorized, and included in performance and failure
accounting.

The eighth is **security by refusal**. Controls block so much legitimate work
that operators route around them, disable monitoring, or move sensitive work
to ungoverned systems. False denial, delay, recovery burden, and reviewer time
belong in the evaluation alongside prevented disclosures and effects.

The ninth is **release ceremony**. A long dossier changes no decision, or a
model card is treated as control after public copies exist. The release process
earns its complexity only when it changes an option, exposes a missing fact,
improves downstream evidence, or assigns a residual that would otherwise be
hidden.

The tenth is **centralized false assurance**. The same vendor, model, policy,
observer, and evaluator produce every favorable record. Redundant signatures
or prompts then look like independent evidence. The trust graph should expose
shared dependencies and route consequential disagreements to a genuinely
different observer where feasible.

## What the Current Evidence Can Establish

The live technical book contains implemented bounded Lean targets and
deterministic fixtures for the seven owners in this chapter. Those artifacts
formalize finite admission rules, identity preservation, named rejection
states, lifecycle ordering, non-authority, revocation limits, and mutation
controls. They are useful because they make some forms of laundering impossible
inside the modeled state machines.

Their limit is equally important. A theorem over a finite custody record does
not establish that every physical copy was discovered. A rejected synthetic
secret leak does not establish prompt-injection resistance or side-channel
security. A protected-execution schema does not establish cryptographic
soundness, hardware trust, or measured leakage. A supply-chain fixture does not
establish a trustworthy supplier or complete dependency graph. A release
review model does not authorize release.

External sources strengthen the vocabulary and objections. Classical
protection principles motivate least privilege and complete mediation. NIST
taxonomies distinguish adversarial-learning stages and attacker capabilities.
Privacy frameworks make purpose, rights, and organizational context visible.
Confidential-computing and remote-attestation architectures separate trust
domains, evidence, appraisal, and relying-party decisions. RAND's model-weight
work emphasizes multiple attack paths and defense in depth. Supply-chain
standards cover lifecycle risk, suppliers, monitoring, and incident response.
These are comparators and design grounding, not local conformance results.

A credible natural evaluation would run the same bounded work through simpler
and richer policies. It would compare ordinary process isolation, a narrow
reference monitor, a protected-computation path, and the composed route. It
would include benign tasks, prompt injection, confused-deputy requests,
dependency substitution, stale attestation, artifact mismatch, privacy-rights
changes, copy creation, revocation, silent-fallback pressure, and release
language that falsely implies recall.

The measurements would include accepted useful completion, unauthorized
effects, secret and inferred disclosure, false denial, missed help, utility
loss, latency, resource cost, reviewer burden, recovery, residual closure, and
complete attempt denominators. Independent implementations should challenge
the monitor, verifier, observer, dependency resolver, and evaluator. Transfer
should span models, tools, hardware, organizations, data rights, attack
families, and time.

Evidence that a materially smaller trusted base matches those outcomes at lower
burden would narrow the architecture. Evidence that ordinary authenticated
encryption, strict access control, minimal logging, short retention, and
independent audit perform as well as advanced protected computation would
remove unnecessary mechanisms. Evidence that release dossiers do not improve
decisions or downstream response would justify a simpler process. The stack is
not entitled to complexity merely because its records are precise.

## From Minimum Implementation to a Mature Security Fabric

The minimum viable implementation can protect one narrow repository task. It
needs an external tool broker, exact principal and artifact identities, a
short-lived capability lease, a temporary workspace, denied-by-default network
and secret access, file-scope enforcement, taint on protected inputs, a separate
commit decision, cleanup, and an append-only receipt. A synthetic secret and a
harmless dependency substitution provide positive and negative controls.

Add privacy by declaring the data categories, purpose, retention, recipients,
known copies, and deletion or restriction route. Add custody by binding the
exact model and derivative identities, storage locations, keys, load purpose,
temporary plaintext surfaces, and closure action. Add supply-chain integrity by
pinning code and dependencies and preserving the path from a changed component
to affected results. Add protected computation only if the named distrust
boundary justifies its cost. Keep public release outside the minimum exercise.

The next level replaces assumed enforcement with independently observed
effects. A separate process watches filesystem and network activity. Artifact
digests are checked at load and commit. A verifier distinct from the workload
appraises attestation or proof evidence. Recovery tests confirm what rollback
actually restores. Revocation propagates to known descendants. False refusals
and operator workarounds are measured, not dismissed.

A mature system would compile stable policy while preserving challenge. It
would maintain a live graph joining principals, purposes, data, models,
dependencies, environments, keys, leases, effects, recipients, releases, and
residuals. Changes in a policy, advisory, model derivative, firmware version,
rights state, or recipient would invalidate only the decisions that depend on
that relation. The system would know which controls remain reversible and
which effects have crossed into compensation or societal response.

The mature kernel would be substrate-aware but not vendor-sovereign. Hardware
roots, cloud attestations, cryptographic proofs, operating-system controls, and
organizational approvals would enter as typed evidence with explicit issuers,
dependencies, freshness, and failure modes. No vendor token would become a
universal trust bit. Multiple mechanisms could be composed when they protect
different properties, and removed when a simpler route performs as well.

At the frontier, security becomes a continuous experimental discipline. New
models, tools, compression methods, memory systems, and deployment surfaces
change the attack and custody graph. The system generates threat hypotheses,
runs bounded adversarial campaigns, learns from incidents, updates controls,
and preserves negative results. Yet the learner cannot rewrite its own
protected floors, erase failed attempts, broaden its authority, or publish a
new release merely because optimization predicts a benefit.

This mature state is beyond what the current repository demonstrates. No
production reference monitor, confidential model deployment, complete artifact
graph, real weight-custody campaign, or open-release experiment has been
validated here. The architecture is a research target whose components must
earn admission against strong simpler baselines.

## The Strongest Objection

The strongest objection is that this machinery can create an elaborate theater
of control. Every transition gains a schema, receipt, signature, proof, policy,
and reviewer, while a compromised operator or overlooked channel defeats the
whole arrangement. Complexity expands the attack surface. Centralized custody
can concentrate power. Restrictive release policy can suppress beneficial open
work. Privacy records can normalize surveillance by making it look governed.
Attestation can transfer trust to opaque hardware and vendors.

This objection has teeth. The answer cannot be another layer of paperwork. A
control belongs only if it changes an effect, exposes a consequential unknown,
improves recovery, or reduces the trusted base under matched evaluation. The
system should prefer ordinary encryption, process isolation, access control,
short retention, and independent audit when they satisfy the declared threat
model. It should preserve open alternatives and distributional benefits in
release decisions. It should minimize sensitive audit data and allow affected
people to contest the purpose, not merely inspect the receipt.

The kernel must also be designed for compromise. Independent observation,
content binding, separation of evidence from authorization, narrow grants,
short expiry, safe holds, rollback, and residual ownership limit how far one
failed component can speak. They do not eliminate root compromise. When the
root or observer cannot be trusted, the system should narrow its claim and
stop the dependent transition rather than manufacture certainty.

The conclusion should change if simpler systems prove equally effective across
the complete joint outcome. It should also change if the governance burden
predictably drives work into less accountable channels. The goal is not maximum
control. It is the smallest enforceable boundary that preserves legitimate
work, human rights, artifact integrity, recoverability, and honest knowledge of
what cannot be controlled.

## What This Establishes

Security, privacy, protected computation, model custody, supply-chain
integrity, and release governance are connected because they share identities
and transitions. They remain separate because they answer different questions.
The kernel governs privileged effects. Adversarial model security governs
threat-relative learned behavior. Privacy governs legitimate information use
and remedy. Protected computation governs named guarantees across distrust
boundaries. Custody governs possession, keys, loads, copies, and retirement.
Supply-chain integrity governs dependencies and invalidation. Open release
governs the point where direct control is intentionally surrendered.

The practical rule is to refuse inference between those properties. A signed
artifact is not necessarily safe. An attested environment is not necessarily
authorized. An authorized use is not necessarily private. A private
computation is not necessarily correct. A robust model is not necessarily
properly constrained. A successful local load is not release authority. A
public license is not universal recall.

For the repository change, this produces a useful outcome even when some gates
stay closed. The paper can be preserved and discussed. Its code can be pinned
or quarantined. Its reported result can remain source-reported. A harmless
local test can be separated from its publication status. Sensitive data can be
excluded. Weights can remain external. Residuals can stay visible. The book can
say exactly what it learned without claiming that the package, model, runtime,
or release is secure.

Secure custody still does not tell the system what to believe. A perfectly
mediated experiment can use a weak construct, a biased evaluator, a stale
source, or an invalid inference. The next chapter turns from control of
information and effects to the governance of evidence itself: how claims gain,
lose, and retain support when review capacity is limited and the system being
evaluated may influence the evaluator.
